reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: A clinical syndrome of bleeding into the alveolar spaces from the pulmonary microcirculation, presenting with breathlessness, cough, hypoxaemia, and diffuse alveolar infiltrates
Haemoptysis may be absent in up to a third of cases, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis
A falling haemoglobin together with new diffuse infiltrates should raise suspicion even without overt bleeding
Bronchoalveolar lavage showing progressively bloodier returns across sequential aliquots, or abundant haemosiderin-laden macrophages, confirms alveolar haemorrhage
The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide is characteristically increased because intra-alveolar blood takes up the tracer gas

Underlying causes include small-vessel vasculitides and capillaritis (such as ANCA-associated vasculitis and anti-GBM disease), connective tissue disease, and non-inflammatory causes such as coagulopathy or mitral stenosis
Management principles are prompt treatment of the underlying cause with immunosuppression for immune-mediated capillaritis, alongside supportive respiratory care
Plasma exchange is used in anti-GBM disease and in severe ANCA-associated haemorrhage
reference.pathophysiology: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage results from disruption of the alveolar-capillary basement membrane allowing red cells to enter the alveoli. The commonest mechanism is pulmonary capillaritis, an immune-mediated neutrophilic inflammation of the small vessels seen in ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, and connective tissue disorders. Bland haemorrhage without inflammation occurs in coagulopathy, anticoagulation, or raised pulmonary venous pressure, and diffuse alveolar damage can also produce bleeding. Regardless of cause, accumulated intra-alveolar blood impairs gas exchange and, if ongoing, causes progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
additionalDifferentials: Severe pneumonia or acute respiratory distress syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Bronchoscopy with sequential bronchoalveolar lavage to confirm haemorrhage and exclude infection
Autoimmune serology including ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, ANA, and complement
Renal function and urinalysis to detect an accompanying pulmonary-renal syndrome
Coagulation studies and echocardiography to assess non-inflammatory causes
redFlags: Rapidly progressive hypoxaemia and respiratory failure requiring urgent airway and ventilatory support - a medical emergency
Concurrent acute kidney injury with active urinary sediment indicating a pulmonary-renal syndrome needing immediate immunosuppression and possibly plasma exchange
Rapidly falling haemoglobin signalling ongoing brisk bleeding
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause and speed of treatment; immune-mediated haemorrhage can be life-threatening but often responds to prompt immunosuppression, while recurrent episodes may cause pulmonary fibrosis, and delayed treatment carries high mortality.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because haemoptysis is absent
Attributing diffuse infiltrates solely to infection or oedema and missing capillaritis
Delaying immunosuppression while awaiting confirmatory serology in a deteriorating patient
Failing to check renal function and urinalysis for an associated pulmonary-renal syndrome
